questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to diagnose TCP pathologies with built-in Linux tools under realistic bursts.

## Key Concepts
- TCP window, backlog, queueing
- Distinguishing client/server/network bottlenecks
- Safe, reversible sysctl tuning with observability checks

## Code Example
```bash
# sample commands
curl -sS -w '%{time_starttransfer}\n' http://localhost/health -o /dev/null
ss -tnae | grep ESTAB
cat /proc/net/tcp | head
tcpdump -i eth0 -c 200 'tcp and port 80'
sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=1024
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_rmem='4096 87380 6291456'
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_wmem='4096 87380 6291456'
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you roll back if no improvement is observed?
- What other netstats would you monitor after changes?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to reason about cgroups resource limits and real-time debugging in a practical, real-world service context.

## Key Concepts

- cgroups memory and CPU quotas
- systemd resource control and slices
- observing usage vs limit via /proc and /sys/fs/cgroup
- safe, incremental mitigations with observability preserved

## Code Example

```bash
# Determine pid
pid=$(pidof myservice)
# Identify cgroup path
grep -a "$pid" /proc/$pid/cgroup
# Read limits and usage
cgrp=$(awk -F: '/memory/ {print $3}' /proc/$pid/cgroup)
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/$cgrp/memory.usage_in_bytes
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/$cgrp/memory.limit_in_bytes
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/$cgrp/cpu.cfs_quota_us
# Apply mitigation
sudo systemctl set-property myservice.MemoryLimit=512M
sudo systemctl set-property myservice.CPUQuota=100000
sudo systemctl restart myservice
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you scale this to multiple services sharing a node?
- How would you validate observability after changes?

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates real-world tail-latency diagnosis in storage-heavy Linux environments using only baseline tools. It tests the ability to correlate I/O queuing, cache behavior, and process attribution into a safe remediation that preserves observability.

## Key Concepts
- Block I/O queuing depth, device saturation, and queue wait times (await)
- Page cache pressure and readahead tuning parameters
- Process-to-device I/O mapping via pidstat and iotop
- cgroup cpuset isolation for separating I/O-heavy workloads

## Diagnostic Workflow
```bash
# Step 1: Observe per-device I/O metrics
iostat -xz 1

# Step 2: Identify queue settings
cat /proc/diskstats
ls -la /sys/block/*/queue/

# Step 3: Map I/O to processes
pidstat -d 1 -p ALL

# Step 4: Apply mitigations
blockdev --setra 4096 /dev/nvme0n1
sysctl -w vm.vfs_cache_pressure=50
echo 0-3 > /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset/io-heavy/cpuset.cpus
```

## Interpretation Guide
- **%util near 100%**: Device saturation causing I/O queuing
- **High avgqu-sz**: Requests queued faster than processed
- **High await**: Combined queue wait + device service time
- **Low cache hit ratio + high pgpgin/s**: Page cache thrashing

## Mitigations Summary
| Parameter | Location | Purpose |
|-----------|----------|--------|
| readahead | blockdev --setra | Pre-fetch sequential data |
| vm.vfs_cache_pressure | sysctl | Control page cache reclamation |
| cpuset.cpus | cgroup | Isolate CPU-bound I/O tasks |
